title: Distributed OCR System
text: Distributed OCR System is a microservices-based optical character recognition system with a gateway pattern, offering both single-character classification and full-word recognition. It has three FastAPI services: a Gateway on port 8000 that routes requests and serves a simple web UI, a Character Service on port 8001 running a custom MobileNetV2 or OCR_CNN model in PyTorch trained on handwritten and printed characters, and a Word Service on port 8002 using EasyOCR for text detection and recognition. It runs locally with a script or in containers with Docker Compose, and is deployed on AWS. It was built as part of an Advanced Machine Learning curriculum and presented in a Cloud Computing course.

title: Distributed OCR System: API, logging and testing
text: In the Distributed OCR System, the gateway exposes a web interface and the endpoints POST /predict/character and POST /predict/word, and each service provides health checks and interactive Swagger documentation. All services use standard Python logging, consolidated into a single app.log when run locally with run_local.sh. The project includes test_system.py to verify all services and OCR accuracy, and test_all.sh to run end-to-end tests in both local and Docker modes. Shared preprocessing and model-loading logic lives in a shared module.

title: Distributed OCR System: AWS deployment
text: In the Distributed OCR System, the gateway is deployed on AWS in the eu-north-1 region. User-uploaded images are stored in Amazon S3, and prediction metadata (filename, S3 key, prediction text, confidence, model type, timestamp) is stored in an Amazon RDS PostgreSQL instance (db.t3.micro). The gateway Docker image is built for linux/amd64, pushed to Amazon ECR and run on Amazon ECS, configured through environment variables for the bucket and database URL, and the predictions table is created automatically at startup. Monitoring uses Amazon CloudWatch: centralized logs for the three services, Container Insights for ECS CPU and memory, and health-check alarms.

title: Toxic Comment Classification using RNN and LSTM
text: Toxic Comment Classification is a deep learning multi-label text classification project that detects six types of toxicity in online comments: toxic, severe_toxic, obscene, threat, insult and identity_hate. One comment can have several labels at once. The project implements and compares a bidirectional RNN and an LSTM in PyTorch on about 159,000 comments. The LSTM was clearly better, reaching a micro F1 of 0.65 against 0.55 for the RNN.
outcome: LSTM micro F1 0.65, macro F1 0.54 vs RNN 0.55 and 0.43

title: Toxic Comment Classification: Data and preprocessing
text: In the Toxic Comment Classification project, the dataset had 159,571 comments; after removing 493 invalid samples, 159,078 remained. Labels are very imbalanced: toxic 15,294, obscene 8,449, insult 7,877, severe_toxic 1,595, identity_hate 1,405 and threat 478 positive samples. Text length analysis showed 95 percent of comments under 230 words, so max_length was set to 100 with truncation and padding. Preprocessing includes normalization, tokenization, replacing URLs and IP addresses with special URL and IP tokens, building a vocabulary with PAD and UNK tokens, and converting tokens to integer IDs.

title: Toxic Comment Classification: Models and training
text: In the Toxic Comment Classification project, two architectures were built. The bidirectional RNN uses an embedding layer, a bidirectional RNN and a fully connected layer with 6 output logits; because sequences are padded, it computes the real length with (x != 0).sum(dim=1) and takes the last valid token instead of a padding position. The LSTM model uses embedding, a 2-layer LSTM and a fully connected layer. LSTM configuration: embedding size 128, hidden dimension 256, 2 layers, 10 epochs, batch size 64, learning rate 0.0001, dropout 0.3, max sequence length 100.
review_note: README heading says BiLSTM but the description and config describe a plain LSTM. Confirm.

title: Toxic Comment Classification: Handling label imbalance and thresholds
text: In the Toxic Comment Classification project, label imbalance was handled with class weighting: positive weights equal to the square root of negative count divided by positive count, passed to BCEWithLogitsLoss, where the square root reduces the size of the raw imbalance ratio. Prediction thresholds such as 0.85 and 0.90 on the sigmoid probabilities were tested, since a lower threshold gives more positive predictions (higher recall) and a higher threshold makes the model more conservative (higher precision).

title: Toxic Comment Classification: Results RNN vs LSTM
text: In the Toxic Comment Classification project, overall F1 scores were: RNN micro 0.55, macro 0.43, weighted 0.55; LSTM micro 0.65, macro 0.54, weighted 0.65. Per-label F1 (RNN vs LSTM): toxic 0.60 vs 0.69, severe_toxic 0.29 vs 0.38, obscene 0.59 vs 0.69, threat 0.31 vs 0.45, insult 0.54 vs 0.62, identity_hate 0.24 vs 0.44. Both models did best on frequent labels (toxic, obscene) and worst on rare labels (threat, identity_hate, severe_toxic), showing the effect of imbalance. The LSTM improved most on identity_hate and threat.

title: SEMSOL: Gaze and Engagement Estimation with Blink Detection
text: SEMSOL performs real-time gaze estimation, engagement scoring and eye-blink detection with deep learning and computer vision, from a webcam or video file. Gaze comes from a deep learning model (backbones such as ResNet-18, ResNet-34 and MobileNetV2; Gaze360 or MPIIGaze datasets). A rule-based engagement scorer gives a 0 to 100 score with 4 levels, from Highly Engaged (75 to 100) to Disengaged (0 to 24), and blinks are detected from facial landmarks with cvzone using an eye aspect ratio. Output shows gaze visualization, engagement score overlay and blink counter, and the processed video can be saved.

title: SEMSOL: Engagement levels and blink detection
text: In SEMSOL, engagement is scored from 0 to 100 and mapped to four levels: level 1 Highly Engaged (75 to 100), level 2 Engaged (50 to 74), level 3 Partially Engaged (25 to 49), level 4 Disengaged (0 to 24). Blink detection uses facial landmarks via cvzone: it measures vertical and horizontal eye distances, computes a ratio to decide whether the eye is closed, and increments a counter per blink. Blink data feeds into the engagement score. Performance tips: use a GPU, reduce resolution or disable blink detection for higher FPS, and use MobileNetV2 for faster inference than ResNet.

title: MobileGaze (upstream gaze-estimation library)
text: MobileGaze (yakhyo/gaze-estimation, by Yakhyokhuja Valikhujaev) is an open-source gaze estimation project that supports ResNet 18/34/50, MobileNet v2 and MobileOne s0-s4 models, built on top of L2CS-Net, with ONNX export and inference and face detection through the uniface library (RetinaFace). Models are trained on Gaze360, with mean absolute error of 12.84 degrees for ResNet-18, 11.33 for ResNet-34, 11.34 for ResNet-50, 13.07 for MobileNet V2 and 12.58 for MobileOne S0. SEMSOL uses the same command-line interface, so it appears to build on this project.
